claims.text: A Cr coating with relatively random grain orientation will provide better high-temperature steam-oxidation resistance than a standard columnar-grained Cr coating on zirconium-alloy cladding.
Changing multi-arc ion-plating parameters can change the grain orientation and microstructure of Cr coatings on Zircaloy-4.
Adjusting substrate temperature, bias, and deposition rate can reliably produce a randomized, non-columnar Cr grain structure.
Columnar grain boundaries in Cr coatings provide rapid diffusion paths for oxygen toward the Zircaloy-4 substrate at high temperature.
Random grain orientation is equivalent to eliminating columnar grain boundaries from the Cr layer.
A relatively random Cr grain orientation promotes formation of a compact and uniform oxidation film.
The protective surface oxide formed on Cr-coated zirconium alloy is Cr2O3.
Formation of a Cr2O3 surface film substantially reduces oxidation kinetics of the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Removing columnar oxygen-diffusion pathways will restrict oxygen transport into the zirconium alloy and thereby slow high-temperature oxidation.
The random-oriented Cr coating will retain its adhesion after neutron irradiation.
Retained post-irradiation adhesion will preserve the coating's suitability for in-service neutron-irradiation conditions.
Cr-coated Zircaloy-4 has substantially better oxidation resistance than uncoated Zircaloy-4 in steam at 800, 1000, and 1200 °C.
High-temperature oxidation protection by Cr coatings is relevant to loss-of-coolant accident conditions.
Standard multi-arc ion-plated Cr coatings typically have columnar grains, strong preferred orientation, and a (001) fiber texture.
Ion or simulated irradiation can be used to assess whether the randomized coating retains adhesion under actual neutron irradiation.
Irradiation-induced microstructural evolution or inadequate deposition control may negate the oxidation-resistance benefit.
